name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q01 - Identify regions of the root tip

questiontext.text: In the given diagram of the regions of a root-tip, identify the regions labelled X and Y.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows the longitudinal view of a root-tip with the thimble-like root cap at the apex, root hairs in the uppermost zone, a compact zone labelled X located a few millimetres above the root cap, and an elongated zone labelled Y located proximal to X and below the root hair zone.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In standard botanical root-tip morphology, zones are described from the distal apex (tip) proximally (upward toward the stem base).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
A typical root-tip is organised sequentially from apex to base into four regions: (i) the root cap protecting the tender apex, (ii) the region of meristematic activity containing small, thin-walled, rapidly dividing cells with dense protoplasm, (iii) the region of elongation whose cells undergo rapid elongation and enlargement for growth in length, and (iv) the region of maturation where cells differentiate and epidermal cells form root hairs.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Label X lies just a few millimetres above the root cap and shows small, densely packed cells; therefore, X represents the region of meristematic activity.
2. Label Y lies immediately proximal to the meristematic zone and below the root hair-bearing region of maturation; therefore, Y represents the region of elongation.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Moving from the root cap upwards, the sequence is root cap, region of meristematic activity (X), region of elongation (Y), and region of maturation. Hence, X is the region of meristematic activity and Y is the region of elongation.

answer.text: X: Region of elongation; Y: Region of maturation
X: Region of meristematic activity; Y: Region of elongation
X: Root cap; Y: Region of meristematic activity
X: Region of maturation; Y: Root cap

questiontext.text: Identify the type of aestivation shown in the given diagram and select the pair of plants that exhibits this arrangement of petals.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows a transverse floral bud representation of five petals arranged in a whorl where the margins of adjacent petals overlap one another, but not in a uniform clockwise or anticlockwise direction.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Each curved arc represents a single petal in cross-section; overlapping ends indicate that one petal margin lies external (outer) to the adjacent petal margin.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Aestivation is the mode of arrangement of sepals or petals in a floral bud with respect to other members of the same whorl. Four major types exist:
1. Valvate: Margins just touch without overlapping (e.g., Calotropis).
2. Twisted: One margin of each appendage consistently overlaps the next in a single direction (e.g., china rose, lady's finger, cotton).
3. Imbricate: Margins overlap one another, but not in any particular direction (e.g., Cassia, gulmohur).
4. Vexillary: Five petals with a large posterior standard overlapping two lateral wings, which in turn overlap two smallest anterior keel petals (e.g., pea, bean).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
In the given diagram, the uppermost petal has both margins lying outside the adjacent petals, whereas the lowermost petal has both margins lying inside the adjacent petals. Thus, overlapping occurs irregularly rather than in one fixed direction or in a papilionaceous (1+2+2) pattern. This defines imbricate aestivation, which is characteristic of Cassia and gulmohur.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Because the overlap is non-directional (not valvate, not uniformly twisted, and not papilionaceous/vexillary), the aestivation is imbricate, found in Cassia and gulmohur.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q03 - Identify placentation type from ovary T.S.

questiontext.text: The given transverse section represents the arrangement of ovules within an ovary. Identify this type of placentation and the plant in which it is found.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The transverse section of the ovary shows a single chamber (unilocular) with ovules borne on placentae located along the inner peripheral wall of the ovary, and no central axis or septa dividing the cavity into locules.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The outer green ring represents the ovary wall, the peripheral projections represent placentae, and the paired oval structures represent ovules attached to those placentae.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Placentation is the arrangement of ovules within the ovary:
- Parietal placentation: Ovules develop on the inner wall of the ovary or on the peripheral part; the ovary is one-chambered (though it may become two-chambered in some cases due to a false septum), as seen in mustard and Argemone.
- Axile placentation: Placenta is axial in a multilocular ovary with septa (e.g., china rose, tomato, lemon).
- Free central placentation: Ovules are borne on a central axis and septa are absent (e.g., Dianthus, Primrose).
- Basal placentation: Placenta develops at the base of the ovary with a single ovule attached (e.g., sunflower, marigold).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since the ovules in the diagram are attached to the inner peripheral wall of the unilocular ovary rather than to a central axis or the base, the arrangement is parietal placentation. Among the given examples, Argemone exhibits parietal placentation, whereas tomato has axile, Dianthus has free central, and sunflower has basal placentation.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The peripheral attachment of ovules on the inner ovary wall confirms parietal placentation, which is found in Argemone.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q04 - Match floral diagram to floral formula

questiontext.text: Observe the given floral diagram carefully. Which of the following floral formulae and plant families accurately corresponds to this diagram?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The floral diagram displays a mother axis dot at the top, an outermost whorl of 5 united sepals, a second whorl of 5 united petals, 5 stamens attached directly to the petals, and a central bilocular ovary placed obliquely with swollen placentae bearing numerous ovules on a central axis.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In floral diagrams and formulae: radial symmetry is represented by \(\oplus\), bisexuality by \(\text{⚥}\), fusion within a whorl by brackets \((\;)\), adhesion between whorls (such as epipetalous stamens) by an arc above the symbols, and a superior ovary by a line below \(\text{G}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. Symmetry and Sexuality: The flower is actinomorphic (\(\oplus\)) and bisexual (\(\text{⚥}\)) as both stamens and carpels are present.
2. Calyx: Five united sepals (gamosepalous) with valvate aestivation \(\rightarrow \text{K}_{(5)}\).
3. Corolla: Five united petals (gamopetalous) with valvate aestivation \(\rightarrow \text{C}_{(5)}\).
4. Androecium: Five stamens attached to the petals (epipetalous) \(\rightarrow \widehat{\text{C}_{(5)} \, \text{A}_5}\).
5. Gynoecium: Bicarpellary, syncarpous, superior ovary, bilocular and obliquely placed with axile placentation \(\rightarrow \underline{\text{G}}_{(2)}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Combining all whorls yields the floral formula \(\oplus \, \text{⚥} \, \text{K}_{(5)} \, \widehat{\text{C}_{(5)} \, \text{A}_5} \, \underline{\text{G}}_{(2)}\). A pentamerous, actinomorphic flower with united calyx and corolla, five epipetalous stamens, and an obliquely placed bicarpellary syncarpous superior ovary with swollen axile placentae is the diagnostic feature of family Solanaceae (e.g., Solanum nigrum).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Brassicaceae has tetramerous \(\text{K}_{2+2}\text{C}_4\text{A}_{2+4}\), Fabaceae has zygomorphic papilionaceous corolla and diadelphous stamens \(\text{A}_{(9)+1}\), and Liliaceae has a trimerous perianth \(\text{P}_{(3+3)}\) and tricarpellary ovary \(\underline{\text{G}}_{(3)}\). Therefore, the diagram corresponds to \(\oplus \, \text{⚥} \, \text{K}_{(5)} \, \widehat{\text{C}_{(5)} \, \text{A}_5} \, \underline{\text{G}}_{(2)}\) of family Solanaceae.
